summary.name: Generic mitigations
summary.one_liner: An O'Reilly essay arguing that services should have ready-made, broadly applicable outage mitigations (such as rollbacks, degrade, drain, and quarantine) so on-call engineers can restore service before fully diagnosing the problem.
keywords: time to fix vs time to mitigate
use_cases: Deciding which emergency mitigations a service needs
Training on-call engineers to use mitigations safely
summary.what_it_does: The essay defines a mitigation as any action that reduces the impact of a production breakage, and a generic mitigation as one useful across many outages. It lists common patterns: rollback, data rollback, degrade, upsize, block list, drain, and quarantine. It argues that generic mitigations let responders act without fully understanding the problem, so the goal is to minimize time to mitigate rather than time to fix. It also notes that these patterns need tailoring per service and diagnosis, and that teams should practice using mitigations through drills, tests, or access checklists.
notable: Frames incident success as time to mitigate rather than time to fix
Catalogues seven generic mitigation patterns with caveats on when each applies
Recommends regularly exercising mitigations so their side effects are known before a real outage
caveats: Generic mitigations are hard to build well and must be tailored to each service
Some patterns, such as draining, do not suit services whose users are pinned to one zone
Mitigations only help if the team has practiced using them
